pass_rule: all core questions substantially correct in the learner's own words; stretch questions inform the grade, not the gate

questions.prompt: Your client gets a 400, a 429, a 503, and a 200 back from four requests. What does each one tell you, and what should the client do about each?
expected_points: 2xx: success — read and decode the body
4xx: the request is wrong; retrying the identical request fails identically, so fix it, don't retry
429 is the 4xx exception: an explicit invitation to slow down and retry later
5xx: the server's problem, likely transient — a retry with backoff can succeed

questions.prompt: Why is an HTTP client without timeouts described as a production incident waiting to happen? Walk through what actually goes wrong.
expected_points: defaults in most libraries (including Go's http.DefaultClient) wait forever
a hung dependency parks a goroutine/socket/memory per in-flight call and they never return
requests pile up, the service stops answering its own callers, and the outage cascades upstream
fix is layered: a client-wide ceiling plus per-request context deadlines

questions.prompt: What happens, concretely, if your client never closes response bodies? And why must the status be checked before decoding?
expected_points: unclosed bodies leak pooled connections: sockets and file descriptors pin up until requests fail or redial from scratch
close on every path, success and error alike
error responses carry HTML or stack traces, not your JSON — decoding first hides the real failure behind a parse error
typed errors (like APIError with the status code) let callers branch on what the server said

questions.prompt: Design a retry policy for a client: which failures do you retry, which do you surface immediately, and how do you decide?
expected_points: retry transport failures (request may never have arrived) and 5xx/429
never retry other 4xx — the request itself is wrong
never retry after context cancellation — the caller already gave up
only requests safe to repeat: idempotent methods like GET/PUT/DELETE; a blind POST retry can e.g. double-charge
cap total attempts and then surface the error

questions.prompt: A thousand clients all get a 503 from the same overloaded server at the same moment. Compare what happens with fixed-interval retries versus exponential backoff with full jitter.
expected_points: fixed interval: all clients retry together — synchronized waves that re-spike the struggling server (thundering herd)
exponential backoff spaces attempts out and gives the server room to recover
jitter (uniform in [0, delay]) desynchronizes clients, flattening the retry load
both parts are needed: backoff alone still retries in waves

questions.prompt: In Go, `resp, err := client.Do(req)` comes back. In which situations is err non-nil, and in which do you get err == nil but still a failure? Why does the distinction matter for retries?
expected_points: err non-nil means no HTTP conversation completed: DNS failure, connection refused, timeout, cancelled context
a 404 or 500 is a completed conversation — err is nil and the failure lives in resp.StatusCode
retry policy treats them differently: transport errors are retryable (request may not have arrived), status errors depend on the code
